# Preparing and exploring longitudinal data in R {#sec-m02}

```{r}
#| include: false
here::i_am("book/en/chapters/02-data-preparation.qmd")
options(width = 76)
```


```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: true
source(here::here("R", "setup.R"))
walk <- load_walk()
```

Most of the time spent on a longitudinal analysis goes into getting the data into a shape that a model can use, and into looking at them carefully before any model is fitted. Errors made here are hard to detect later. A duplicated visit makes a participant look more precisely measured than they are, a wrongly parsed date puts a measurement at the wrong time, and a missing visit that silently disappears from a table hides the dropout that will drive the main analytical problem of the study. This module takes the WALK trial from a messy visit-level export to a checked analysis file, then describes and plots the data in the ways that matter for longitudinal questions. It ends with a warning that runs through the rest of the course: when people with higher blood pressure leave the study, the average of the people who remain is not the average of everyone randomised.

## Learning outcomes {.unnumbered}

By the end of this module participants will be able to:

1. **2.1** Reshape longitudinal data between long and wide formats with `tidyr`, keeping identifiers and time variables intact.
2. **2.2** Join visit-level and participant-level files and validate the result: unique subject–visit keys, consistent identifiers and plausible values.
3. **2.3** Detect and resolve exact and conflicting duplicate records, missing visits and discrepancies between scheduled and actual measurement times, and document each decision.
4. **2.4** Produce baseline summaries by group, visit-specific summaries and a participant-flow table.
5. **2.5** Construct and interpret spaghetti plots, individual trajectory panels, group mean plots and missingness plots.
6. **2.6** Explain why observed group means at each visit are not the same as model-estimated mean trajectories when dropout depends on the outcome.

## Prerequisites {.unnumbered}

Module 1 (the vocabulary of participants, observations, visits and measurement occasions, and the WALK design). Module 0 covers the `dplyr` and `ggplot2` basics used here.

::: {.callout-warning title="Simulated data"}
All examples use simulated data from fictional studies. Results illustrate methods; they are not empirical findings.
:::

The WALK files used in this module are:

| File | One row per | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| `walk_wide.csv` | participant | reshaping |
| `walk_long.csv` | attended visit | the checked analysis file |
| `walk_baseline.csv` | participant | joins, randomisation dates, dropout information |
| `walk_visits_raw.csv` | record in a messy export | the cleaning workflow |
| `walk_complete.csv` | scheduled visit, before missingness | teaching only: shows what the missing values were |

```{r}
#| label: load-files
baseline <- load_walk("baseline")
wide     <- load_walk("wide")
sched_months <- c(0, 1, 3, 6, 9, 12)
```

## Long and wide formats

### The research question and estimand

Reshaping does not answer a scientific question by itself, but every question in the course needs data in a particular shape. Mixed models, generalized estimating equations and most plots need **long format**: one row per observation, with an identifier, a time variable and the outcome. Some summaries, correlation matrices between visits and certain imputation methods need **wide format**: one row per participant and one column per scheduled visit. The task is to move between the two without losing or inventing information.

### Data structure and outcome types

`walk_wide.csv` has `r nrow(wide)` rows and the columns `sbp_m0` to `sbp_m12`, one per scheduled month. The analysis file `walk_long.csv` has `r nrow(walk)` rows, one per attended visit, with `visit`, the scheduled month `month_sched` and the actual month `month`.

```{r}
#| label: show-wide
head(wide, 4)
```

The identifier (`id`) defines the subject. The **scheduled time** (`month_sched`) defines the visit. The **actual time** (`month`) is when the measurement was really taken. A wide file can carry only one of these as column names, and it is always the scheduled one.

### Intuition

A wide file is a table of participants by visits. A long file stacks the columns of that table on top of each other and records, in a new column, which visit each value came from. Reshaping wide to long therefore needs three pieces of information: which columns hold the repeated measurements, how to turn each column name into a time value, and what to call the column of values. Reshaping long to wide needs the reverse: which column supplies the new column names and which supplies the values. Anything that varies within a participant but is not named in the reshape (for example actual time or steps) cannot fit in a single wide row and has to be dropped or reshaped into its own set of columns.

### The model

There is no statistical model here, but it helps to state the correspondence exactly. For participant $i$ the wide row holds the vector

$$
\mathbf{y}_i = (y_{i1}, y_{i2}, \dots, y_{i6})^\top ,
$$

where $y_{ij}$ is SBP at scheduled visit $j$ and some elements may be missing. The long file holds one row for each pair $(i, j)$ with columns $(i,\; s_j,\; y_{ij})$, where $s_j \in \{0, 1, 3, 6, 9, 12\}$ is the scheduled month of visit $j$. The pair $(i, s_j)$ is the **key**: it must identify exactly one row. Moving from wide to long creates $N \times 6$ rows, of which the missing $y_{ij}$ may be kept as explicit `NA` rows or dropped. The actual time $t_{ij}$ is extra information that the wide format has no place for.

### Assumptions and limitations

Reshaping assumes that the key is unique (no participant has two values for the same visit) and that column names encode the time consistently. Wide format assumes a common schedule. It cannot represent actual measurement times that differ between participants, or unscheduled extra visits, without adding further columns. It also hides missing visits less obviously than one might expect: an `NA` cell is visible, but a long file that simply lacks a row gives no sign of the absent visit.

### Fitting the model in R

`tidyr::pivot_longer()` goes from wide to long. `names_prefix` strips the text `sbp_m` from the column names and `names_transform` turns what remains into a number.

```{r}
#| label: pivot-longer
long_from_wide <- wide |>
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("sbp_m"),
               names_to = "month_sched", names_prefix = "sbp_m",
               names_transform = list(month_sched = as.numeric),
               values_to = "sbp")
long_from_wide
```

`tidyr::pivot_wider()` goes back. Only variables that are constant within a participant (`clinic`, `arm`, `age`, `sex`, `bmi`) may stay as identifying columns. If `month` or `steps` were left in, every visit would have a different value and `pivot_wider()` would produce one row per visit instead of one per participant.

```{r}
#| label: pivot-wider
wide_again <- walk |>
  select(id, clinic, arm, age, sex, bmi, month_sched, sbp) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = month_sched, values_from = sbp,
              names_prefix = "sbp_m")
dim(wide_again)
```

### Interpreting the output

```{r}
#| label: reshape-counts
n_long_rows <- nrow(long_from_wide)
n_long_na   <- sum(is.na(long_from_wide$sbp))
reshape_check <- long_from_wide |>
  filter(!is.na(sbp)) |>
  full_join(walk |> select(id, month_sched, sbp_long = sbp),
            by = c("id", "month_sched"))
n_mismatch <- sum(is.na(reshape_check$sbp) | is.na(reshape_check$sbp_long) |
                    reshape_check$sbp != reshape_check$sbp_long)
```

The long version of the wide file has `r n_long_rows` rows ($`r nrow(wide)` \times 6$), of which `r n_long_na` hold `NA` because the visit was not attended. Dropping those leaves `r n_long_rows - n_long_na` rows, the same number as `walk_long.csv`. Matching the two by `id` and `month_sched` finds `r n_mismatch` disagreements in SBP. The round trip back to wide gives `r nrow(wide_again)` rows and `r ncol(wide_again)` columns, the same shape as the original wide file.

| Output | What it means | Value here |
|---|---|---|
| Rows after `pivot_longer()` | participants × scheduled visits | `r n_long_rows` |
| `NA` values | scheduled visits not attended | `r n_long_na` |
| Rows after dropping `NA` | attended visits | `r n_long_rows - n_long_na` |
| SBP disagreements with `walk_long` | errors introduced by reshaping | `r n_mismatch` |

### Checking the model

Check every reshape in both directions. Count rows before and after, check that the number of distinct identifiers has not changed, and compare values with an independent source where one exists. `all.equal()` compares two data frames value by value:

```{r}
#| label: reshape-allequal
all.equal(as.data.frame(wide_again), as.data.frame(wide),
          check.attributes = FALSE)
```

If `pivot_wider()` warns that "values are not uniquely identified" and produces list-columns, the key is not unique. That is a duplicate problem to solve before reshaping (see the cleaning section below), not something to fix with `values_fn = mean`.

### Reporting

Reshaping is rarely mentioned in a paper, but the analysis log should record it: "The wide file (`r nrow(wide)` participants) was converted to long format (`r n_long_rows` participant-visits, `r n_long_rows - n_long_na` with an observed SBP). Converting back reproduced the original file exactly."

::: {.callout-important title="Common mistakes"}
- **Leaving time-varying columns in `pivot_wider()`.** The result has one row per visit, full of `NA`. Select only the key, the time and the value (plus constant covariates) first.
- **Keeping the time as text.** `"m12"` sorts before `"m3"`. Use `names_prefix` and `names_transform` so that time is numeric.
- **Treating scheduled time as actual time.** The wide file cannot hold actual times. Join them back from the long file when the analysis uses actual time.
- **Dropping `NA` rows without counting them.** Record how many visits were missing before you discard the rows.
:::

## Joining participant-level and visit-level files

### The research question and estimand

Analyses need participant-level information (arm, baseline covariates, randomisation date, dropout status) on every visit row. A **join** copies it from the participant-level file onto the visit-level file. The aim is a long file in which every row has the right participant's covariates, and no rows have been created or lost.

### Data structure and outcome types

`walk_baseline.csv` has one row per participant (`r nrow(baseline)` rows, key `id`). The visit file has one row per participant and visit. This is a **many-to-one** relationship: many visit rows match one baseline row.

### Intuition

A join looks up each visit row's `id` in the baseline file and appends the matching columns. Three things can go wrong. An `id` in the visit file may have no match (a typing error, a lower-case ID, a participant missing from the baseline file), and a left join will then fill the new columns with `NA` without complaint. An `id` may appear twice in the baseline file, and every visit for that participant is then duplicated. Or both files may contain the same variable (`arm`, `age`), and the join creates `arm.x` and `arm.y` that may silently disagree.

### The model

Write the participant-level covariates as $\mathbf{x}_i$ and the visit-level data as $(y_{ij}, t_{ij})$. A correct join produces rows $(i, j, y_{ij}, t_{ij}, \mathbf{x}_i)$: the participant-level values are repeated, unchanged, on each of the $n_i$ rows of participant $i$. Formally the baseline file must define a function $i \mapsto \mathbf{x}_i$, which means that each $i$ appears at most once. The number of rows after a left join equals the number before it only if that holds.

### Assumptions and limitations

The join assumes that the key is spelled the same way in both files (same case, no stray spaces, same type) and is unique in the participant-level file. It does not check that the values make sense. A baseline file with the wrong arm for one participant will be joined without complaint.

### Fitting the model in R

`dplyr::left_join()` keeps every row of the left (visit) file. The `relationship` argument states what you expect. With `"many-to-one"`, dplyr stops with an error if any `id` occurs more than once in the right-hand file. Select only the variables you need from the baseline file, so that no name is duplicated.

```{r}
#| label: join
walk_joined <- walk |>
  left_join(baseline |> select(id, rand_date, sbp0, dropout, last_month_sched),
            by = "id", relationship = "many-to-one")
c(before = nrow(walk), after = nrow(walk_joined))
```

`anti_join()` lists keys that do not match, in each direction:

```{r}
#| label: anti-join
nrow(anti_join(walk, baseline, by = "id"))   # visit rows without a baseline row
nrow(anti_join(baseline, walk, by = "id"))   # randomised but never seen
```

To see the `relationship` check at work, duplicate one baseline row deliberately:

```{r}
#| label: join-error
baseline_bad <- bind_rows(baseline, baseline |> filter(id == "W001"))
res <- tryCatch(
  left_join(walk, baseline_bad |> select(id, rand_date),
            by = "id", relationship = "many-to-one"),
  error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
cat(res)
```

### Interpreting the output

The join kept `r nrow(walk_joined)` rows, exactly the number in `walk_long`. Both anti-joins return zero rows: every visit belongs to a randomised participant, and every randomised participant has at least the baseline visit. The deliberately corrupted baseline file produced an error naming the offending row. Without `relationship`, dplyr would only have warned, and W001's visits would have appeared twice.

### Checking the model

After every join, check:

1. the row count is unchanged (for a many-to-one left join);
2. no new `NA` values appeared in the joined columns (`sum(is.na(walk_joined$rand_date))` is `r sum(is.na(walk_joined$rand_date))`);
3. no `.x`/`.y` columns were created;
4. the participant-level values are constant within participant, for example `walk_joined |> group_by(id) |> summarise(k = n_distinct(sbp0))` has all `k` equal to 1.

```{r}
#| label: join-constant
walk_joined |> group_by(id) |> summarise(k = n_distinct(sbp0)) |> count(k)
```

### Reporting

"Participant-level data (`r nrow(baseline)` participants) were joined to the visit file by participant identifier. All visit records matched a randomised participant and no participant identifier was duplicated."

::: {.callout-important title="Common mistakes"}
- **Joining on a key with inconsistent case or spaces.** `"w004"` does not match `"W004"`. Standardise keys before joining.
- **Not stating the relationship.** Use `relationship = "many-to-one"` so that a duplicated participant row stops the code.
- **Joining variables that already exist.** `arm.x` and `arm.y` appear. Select the new columns only, or join by all shared columns deliberately.
- **Using `inner_join()` without counting.** An inner join silently drops unmatched rows. Use a left join and inspect the unmatched keys with `anti_join()`.
:::

## Cleaning a raw visit export

Real exports rarely look like `walk_long.csv`. The file `walk_visits_raw.csv` is a deliberately untidy version of the same visits, with the problems that a trial database or a clinic spreadsheet typically produces. This section works through it step by step and records every decision.

### The research question and estimand

The target is an analysis file in which each row is one attended visit of one randomised participant, with a unique key $(i, j)$, a correctly parsed date, the actual time since randomisation, numeric outcome and covariate values, and flags for every value that was changed or questioned. The cleaning must not change the estimand. Rules that depend on outcomes or on arm can do exactly that, so they are fixed before anyone looks at results by arm.

### Data structure and outcome types

```{r}
#| label: read-raw
raw <- read_csv(here("data", "walk_visits_raw.csv"),
                col_types = cols(.default = col_character()))
raw
```

Every column is read as text. That is deliberate: if `read_csv()` guessed the types, a single stray character in `sbp_mmhg` would turn the whole column into text, or a parsing problem would turn a value into `NA` with only a warning. Reading as text and converting explicitly lets you see and count each problem. The file has `r nrow(raw)` rows. `walk_long.csv` has `r nrow(walk)`, so there are `r nrow(raw) - nrow(walk)` more rows than attended visits.

### Intuition

Cleaning is a sequence of small, checkable transformations, each followed by a test. The order matters. Identifiers must be standardised before looking for duplicates, because `w004` and `W004` are the same participant. Exact duplicates must be removed before conflicting duplicates are counted, otherwise a pair of identical rows looks like a conflict. Dates must be parsed before actual time can be derived. Every change is recorded in a log so that another analyst could repeat it.

### The model

Let $D_{ij}$ be the visit date of participant $i$ at scheduled visit $j$, $D^{\text{rand}}_i$ the randomisation date and $s_j$ the scheduled month. WALK defines a month as 30.44 days ($365.25/12$ rounded to two decimals). The actual time is

$$
t_{ij} = \frac{D_{ij} - D^{\text{rand}}_i}{30.44},
$$

in months. The visit was due on the target date $D^{\text{rand}}_i + \operatorname{round}(30.44\, s_j)$, and the deviation in days is

$$
d_{ij} = D_{ij} - \bigl(D^{\text{rand}}_i + \operatorname{round}(30.44\, s_j)\bigr).
$$

A visit is **out of window** if $|d_{ij}| > w_j$, where $w_j$ is the half-width of the protocol window for visit $j$. A value $y_{ij}$ is **implausible** if it lies outside a range fixed in advance, here $[70, 250]$ mmHg for SBP. These quantities are what the code below computes.

### Assumptions and limitations

Each rule rests on an assumption that should be written down. Converting IDs to upper case assumes that `w004` and `W004` are the same person, which is safe only because the protocol format is `W` followed by three digits. Treating rows identical in every column as copies assumes that two genuine measurements cannot agree exactly on date, SBP and steps. The rule for conflicting duplicates is a convention. Without the source documents nobody knows which record is right. Plausibility limits catch gross errors only. A value of 160 entered instead of 150 is plausible and will never be detected by a range check.

### Fitting the model in R

**Step 1. Standardise identifiers and visit labels.** `toupper(trimws())` removes case and spacing differences. The visit label `M12` becomes the scheduled month 12 and visit number 6. The `stopifnot()` lines stop the code if any ID does not match the protocol format or any label is unknown.

```{r}
#| label: clean-ids
raw |> filter(participant != toupper(participant)) |> distinct(participant)

step1 <- raw |>
  mutate(id          = toupper(trimws(participant)),
         month_sched = as.numeric(sub("^M", "", visit_label)),
         visit       = match(month_sched, sched_months))
stopifnot(all(grepl("^W[0-9]{3}$", step1$id)), !anyNA(step1$visit))
```

**Step 2. Parse dates and convert text to numbers.** `as.Date()` with an explicit format returns `NA` for anything that does not match. `readr::parse_double()` converts text to numbers and reports problems.

```{r}
#| label: clean-parse
step2 <- step1 |>
  mutate(visit_date = as.Date(visit_date, format = "%Y-%m-%d"),
         sbp        = parse_double(sbp_mmhg),
         steps      = parse_double(steps_k)) |>
  select(id, visit, month_sched, visit_date, sbp, steps)
c(bad_dates = sum(is.na(step2$visit_date)), missing_sbp = sum(is.na(step2$sbp)),
  missing_steps = sum(is.na(step2$steps)))
```

```{r}
#| label: blank-row
step2 |> filter(is.na(sbp))
```

One SBP value is missing. In the raw file the cell is empty, and `read_csv()` turns empty strings into `NA` by default. This is a **missing value at an attended visit**: the participant came, steps were recorded, but SBP was not entered. It is different from a missed visit and should be queried with the clinic.

**Step 3. Remove exact duplicates.** Rows that agree in every column are copies of one record.

```{r}
#| label: clean-exact
n_exact_dup <- sum(duplicated(step2))
step2[duplicated(step2) | duplicated(step2, fromLast = TRUE), ] |>
  arrange(id, visit)
step3 <- distinct(step2)
```

There are `r n_exact_dup` exact duplicate rows. Removing them leaves `r nrow(step3)` rows.

**Step 4. Find and resolve conflicting duplicates.** After removing exact copies, any remaining repeat of the key $(i, j)$ is a conflict: two different records for the same visit.

```{r}
#| label: clean-conflicts
conflicts <- step3 |>
  add_count(id, visit, name = "n_records") |>
  filter(n_records > 1) |>
  arrange(id, visit, visit_date)
conflicts
```

```{r}
#| label: conflict-numbers
#| include: false
conf_diff <- conflicts |> group_by(id, visit) |>
  summarise(d_sbp = diff(sbp), d_days = as.numeric(diff(visit_date)))
```

There are `r n_distinct(paste(conflicts$id, conflicts$visit))` visits with two records each. Within each pair the dates differ by `r unique(conf_diff$d_days)` days and SBP differs by between `r min(abs(conf_diff$d_sbp))` and `r max(abs(conf_diff$d_sbp))` mmHg. Some rule is needed to keep one record per visit. The best option is to query the clinic and use the source document. When that is impossible, common conventions are to keep the earliest record (the first measurement taken in the visit window), to keep the record closest to the target date, or to average the two values. WALK's data management plan specifies the first: **keep the earliest-dated record and flag the visit**.

The rule must be set without looking at outcomes by arm. Suppose an analyst looked at the three pairs, saw which version made the enhanced programme look better, and chose a rule accordingly. With three pairs the effect would be tiny, but the principle scales: a rule chosen after seeing its consequences is part of the analysis, and it can bias the estimated treatment effect in a direction the analyst prefers. The same applies to outlier removal and window definitions. This is why trial guidelines expect data-handling rules to be written into the statistical analysis plan before unblinding [@gamble2017].

```{r}
#| label: clean-resolve
step4 <- step3 |>
  group_by(id, visit) |>
  mutate(conflict_flag = n() > 1) |>
  arrange(visit_date, .by_group = TRUE) |>
  slice(1) |>
  ungroup()
stopifnot(nrow(count(step4, id, visit) |> filter(n > 1)) == 0)
nrow(step4)
```

**Step 5. Derive actual time.** Join the randomisation date and apply the formulas above. `unmatched = "error"` stops the code if any visit has no baseline row.

```{r}
#| label: clean-time
days_per_month <- 30.44
step5 <- step4 |>
  left_join(baseline |> select(id, rand_date),
            by = "id", relationship = "many-to-one", unmatched = "error") |>
  mutate(days        = as.numeric(visit_date - rand_date),
         month       = round(days / days_per_month, 2),
         target_date = rand_date + round(month_sched * days_per_month),
         dev_days    = as.numeric(visit_date - target_date))
stopifnot(all(step5$days >= 0), all(step5$month[step5$visit == 1] == 0))
```

The checks confirm that no visit is dated before randomisation and that every baseline visit took place on the randomisation date.

**Step 6. Check plausibility.** The range 70–250 mmHg was fixed in advance as plausible for adults with raised blood pressure.

```{r}
#| label: clean-plausible
step5 |> filter(sbp < 70 | sbp > 250)
```

```{r}
#| label: clean-plausible-fix
#| include: false
bad_row <- step5 |> filter(sbp > 250)
```

One value, `r bad_row$sbp` mmHg for `r bad_row$id` at month `r bad_row$month_sched`, is impossible. It looks like `r bad_row$sbp / 10` with an extra zero (a typing error multiplying the value by 10). It is tempting to correct it, and some data management plans allow obvious transcription errors to be corrected. WALK's plan does not, so the value is set to missing, the raw value is kept in a separate column, and a query is logged. If the clinic confirms `r bad_row$sbp / 10`, the correction is made in the database and the cleaning code is rerun.

```{r}
#| label: clean-flag
step6 <- step5 |>
  mutate(sbp_flag = case_when(is.na(sbp) ~ "blank",
                              sbp < 70 | sbp > 250 ~ "implausible",
                              TRUE ~ "ok"),
         sbp_raw = sbp,
         sbp     = if_else(sbp_flag == "implausible", NA_real_, sbp))
count(step6, sbp_flag)
```

**Step 7. Compare scheduled and actual times.** The (hypothetical) WALK protocol allows ±7 days around month 1, ±14 days around month 3 and ±28 days around months 6, 9 and 12.

```{r}
#| label: clean-window
window_days <- c(`0` = 0, `1` = 7, `3` = 14, `6` = 28, `9` = 28, `12` = 28)
walk_clean <- step6 |>
  mutate(window = window_days[as.character(month_sched)],
         out_of_window = abs(dev_days) > window) |>
  select(id, visit, month_sched, visit_date, rand_date, month, dev_days,
         out_of_window, sbp, sbp_raw, sbp_flag, steps, conflict_flag) |>
  arrange(id, visit)

window_table <- walk_clean |>
  filter(visit > 1) |>
  group_by(month_sched) |>
  summarise(window = first(window_days[as.character(month_sched)]),
            n = n(), min_dev = min(dev_days), max_dev = max(dev_days),
            sd_dev = round(sd(dev_days), 1), n_out = sum(out_of_window))
window_table
```

### Interpreting the output

The window table shows that timing becomes more variable as follow-up goes on. The standard deviation of the deviation from the target date grows from `r window_table$sd_dev[1]` days at month 1 to `r window_table$sd_dev[5]` days at month 12, and the most extreme visit is `r max(abs(c(window_table$min_dev, window_table$max_dev)))` days from its target. In total `r sum(walk_clean$out_of_window)` visits (`r round(100 * mean(walk_clean$out_of_window[walk_clean$visit > 1]), 1)`% of follow-up visits) fall outside the window. The decision is to **keep them and flag them**. Excluding them would throw away valid measurements and create extra missing data. Because the course models use actual time (`month`) for the random slope, a visit at 13.2 months is placed at 13.2 months, not at 12. Analyses that use the scheduled visit as a factor treat it as a month-12 measurement. A sensitivity analysis that excludes out-of-window visits can show whether that matters.

```{r}
#| label: clean-log
cleaning_log <- tibble(
  step = c("Rows read", "Exact duplicate rows removed",
           "Rows after removing exact duplicates",
           "Visits with conflicting records", "Rows after resolving conflicts",
           "Blank SBP values", "Implausible SBP values set to missing",
           "Out-of-window visits (kept, flagged)"),
  n = c(nrow(raw), n_exact_dup, nrow(step3),
        n_distinct(paste(conflicts$id, conflicts$visit)), nrow(walk_clean),
        sum(walk_clean$sbp_flag == "blank"),
        sum(walk_clean$sbp_flag == "implausible"),
        sum(walk_clean$out_of_window)))
knitr::kable(cleaning_log, caption = "Cleaning log for walk_visits_raw.csv")
```

The cleaning log is the main output of this section. Together with a query log (one line per questioned value, with the action taken), it lets anyone reproduce the analysis file and see every decision.

### Checking the model

Because WALK is simulated, the checked analysis file `walk_long.csv` exists and the cleaned data can be compared with it. In a real study the equivalent check is double data entry, source-document verification of a sample, or comparison with a previous data freeze.

```{r}
#| label: clean-agree
agreement <- walk_clean |>
  full_join(walk |> select(id, visit, month_ref = month, sbp_ref = sbp,
                           steps_ref = steps), by = c("id", "visit"))
sbp_differs <- agreement |>
  filter(is.na(sbp) | is.na(sbp_ref) | sbp != sbp_ref)
month_diff <- agreement$month - agreement$month_ref
c(only_clean = sum(is.na(agreement$month_ref)),
  only_walk_long = sum(is.na(agreement$month)),
  sbp_differs = nrow(sbp_differs),
  steps_differs = sum(agreement$steps != agreement$steps_ref))
sbp_differs |> select(id, visit, sbp, sbp_raw, sbp_ref, sbp_flag)
table(round(month_diff, 2))
```

The cleaned file has `r nrow(walk_clean)` rows, the same keys as `walk_long.csv`, and identical steps values. SBP differs in exactly `r nrow(sbp_differs)` rows: the blank value and the implausible value, both of which we set to missing while `walk_long.csv` holds the true values. Actual time differs in `r sum(abs(month_diff) > 0.001)` of `r length(month_diff)` rows, but never by more than `r round(max(abs(month_diff)), 2)` months (well under one day). The difference is a rounding artefact that we can explain exactly. The raw file was built by adding `round(month * 30.44)` days to the randomisation date, so the visit date was rounded to a whole day and the original two-decimal month cannot be recovered from it. Our `month` is the correct time of the recorded date. These small differences are honest and harmless, and the report should say so rather than force the two files to agree.

### Reporting

```{r}
#| label: report-numbers
#| include: false
n_out <- sum(walk_clean$out_of_window)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Reporting example"}
The raw visit export contained `r nrow(raw)` records. After identifiers were converted to upper case, `r n_exact_dup` exact duplicate records were removed. `r n_distinct(paste(conflicts$id, conflicts$visit))` visits had two conflicting records; following the prespecified rule, the earliest-dated record was retained and the visit flagged. One SBP value was blank and one (`r bad_row$sbp` mmHg) was implausible; both were treated as missing and queried. Actual time since randomisation was calculated from visit and randomisation dates. `r n_out` follow-up visits (`r round(100 * mean(walk_clean$out_of_window[walk_clean$visit > 1]), 1)`%) were outside the protocol window and were retained, with time modelled as actual time. The analysis file contained `r nrow(walk_clean)` visits from `r n_distinct(walk_clean$id)` participants.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Common mistakes"}
- **Looking for duplicates before standardising IDs.** Copies that differ only in case are missed.
- **Letting `read_csv()` guess types on a messy file.** Problems turn into silent `NA` values. Read as text, convert explicitly and count the failures.
- **Choosing the duplicate or outlier rule after looking at results by arm.** Fix the rule in the analysis plan, before unblinding.
- **Deleting out-of-window visits.** They are valid measurements at a different time. Use actual time and flag them.
- **"Correcting" values without a documented rule.** Keep the raw value, set the cleaned value to missing and raise a query, unless the plan allows the correction.
- **Overwriting the raw file.** Cleaning code reads the raw export and writes a new file. The raw file is never edited by hand.
:::

## Missing visits, summaries and participant flow

From here on the module uses the checked analysis file `walk_long.csv` (loaded as `walk`), so that the numbers agree with the rest of the course.

### The research question and estimand

Before modelling we need to know who was randomised, who was seen at each visit, how the groups compared at baseline and what the outcome looked like at each visit. These are descriptive targets: counts, proportions, means and standard deviations, computed for the right denominators.

### Data structure and outcome types

A long file holds attended visits only, so missed visits are invisible in it. To count them, build the **complete grid** of every randomised participant crossed with every scheduled visit, from the design: `r nrow(baseline)` participants × 6 visits. Do not build the grid from the data (a participant never seen would be lost) and do not use `walk_complete.csv`, which no real study has.

### Intuition

Two kinds of missing visit behave differently. **Intermittent missingness** means a participant missed a visit and came back later. **Dropout** means a participant was never seen again after some visit. Dropout gives a **monotone** pattern: once missing, always missing. The distinction matters because dropout usually has stronger links to the outcome and accumulates over time.

### The model

Let $R_{ij} = 1$ if $y_{ij}$ is observed and $0$ otherwise. For participant $i$ let $L_i = \max\{j : R_{ij} = 1\}$ be the last attended visit. A missing visit $j$ is intermittent if $j < L_i$ and follows dropout if $j > L_i$. The observed mean SBP in arm $g$ at visit $j$ is

$$
\bar{y}_{gj} = \frac{\sum_{i \in g} R_{ij}\, y_{ij}}{\sum_{i \in g} R_{ij}},
$$

the average over those seen. Its denominator changes from visit to visit.

### Assumptions and limitations

The grid assumes that the schedule in the protocol applies to everyone. Descriptive tables of observed data are exactly that: they describe the people who were measured, not the people randomised. Baseline tables in randomised trials describe the groups. Significance tests of baseline differences between randomised arms are not meaningful, because any difference is due to chance by construction.

### Fitting the model in R

```{r}
#| label: grid
grid <- baseline |>
  select(id, arm) |>
  crossing(visit = seq_along(sched_months)) |>
  mutate(month_sched = sched_months[visit]) |>
  left_join(walk |> select(id, visit, sbp), by = c("id", "visit")) |>
  mutate(observed = !is.na(sbp)) |>
  group_by(id) |>
  mutate(last_seen = max(visit[observed]),
         miss_type = case_when(observed ~ "observed",
                               visit < last_seen ~ "intermittent",
                               TRUE ~ "after dropout")) |>
  ungroup()
grid |> count(arm, miss_type) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = miss_type, values_from = n)
```

A baseline table by arm, with a small helper for mean (SD):

```{r}
#| label: baseline-table
mean_sd <- function(x, digits = 1) {
  sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f (%.", digits, "f)"),
          mean(x, na.rm = TRUE), sd(x, na.rm = TRUE))
}
baseline_table <- baseline |>
  group_by(arm) |>
  summarise(n = as.character(n()),
            `Age, years` = mean_sd(age),
            `Female, n (%)` = sprintf("%d (%.0f%%)", sum(sex == "Female"),
                                      100 * mean(sex == "Female")),
            `BMI, kg/m2` = mean_sd(bmi),
            `SBP, mmHg` = mean_sd(sbp0),
            `Steps, 1000/day` = mean_sd(steps0)) |>
  pivot_longer(-arm, names_to = "Characteristic") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = arm, values_from = value)
knitr::kable(baseline_table, caption = "Baseline characteristics by arm, mean (SD) unless stated")
```

Visit-specific summaries, and a participant-flow table built with the course helper `visit_flow()`:

```{r}
#| label: visit-summary
visit_summary <- walk |>
  group_by(arm, month_sched) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(sbp), sd = sd(sbp), mean_month = mean(month))
visit_summary |> filter(arm == "EP")

flow <- visit_flow(walk, id, month_sched, arm) |>
  left_join(count(baseline, arm, name = "randomised"), by = "arm") |>
  mutate(cell = sprintf("%d (%.0f%%)", n_seen, 100 * n_seen / randomised)) |>
  select(arm, month_sched, cell) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = arm, values_from = cell)
knitr::kable(flow, caption = "Participants seen at each scheduled visit, n (% of randomised)")
```

### Interpreting the output

```{r}
#| label: grid-numbers
#| include: false
n_missing <- sum(!grid$observed)
n_interm  <- sum(grid$miss_type == "intermittent")
n_after   <- sum(grid$miss_type == "after dropout")
drop_tab  <- baseline |> group_by(arm) |> summarise(n = sum(dropout), pct = 100 * mean(dropout))
seen12    <- grid |> filter(month_sched == 12) |> group_by(arm) |> summarise(p = 100 * mean(observed))
```

The grid has `r nrow(grid)` scheduled visits, of which `r n_missing` (`r round(100 * n_missing / nrow(grid), 1)`%) are missing: `r n_interm` intermittent and `r n_after` after dropout. Dropout (last attended visit before month 12) occurred in `r drop_tab$n[1]` UC, `r drop_tab$n[2]` SP and `r drop_tab$n[3]` EP participants. The flow table shows attendance falling steadily, to between `r round(min(seen12$p))`% and `r round(max(seen12$p))`% at month 12.

The baseline table shows groups that are similar, as randomisation should produce. Mean baseline SBP is `r round(mean(baseline$sbp0[baseline$arm == "UC"]), 1)`, `r round(mean(baseline$sbp0[baseline$arm == "SP"]), 1)` and `r round(mean(baseline$sbp0[baseline$arm == "EP"]), 1)` mmHg in the three arms. The proportion of women differs by several percentage points between arms. That is chance variation, not a reason for a test. It is a reason to consider adjusting for sex if it is prognostic, as the course's covariate-adjusted model does.

The visit summary for the enhanced programme shows mean SBP falling from `r round(visit_summary$mean[visit_summary$arm == "EP" & visit_summary$month_sched == 0], 1)` mmHg at baseline to `r round(visit_summary$mean[visit_summary$arm == "EP" & visit_summary$month_sched == 12], 1)` mmHg at month 12, with the number of observations falling from 120 to `r visit_summary$n[visit_summary$arm == "EP" & visit_summary$month_sched == 12]`. The column `mean_month` shows that the average actual time at each visit is close to the scheduled time, so the irregular timing does not shift the visits systematically.

### Checking the model

The grid must have exactly $N \times 6$ rows, the number of observed cells must equal the number of rows in the long file (`r sum(grid$observed)` and `r nrow(walk)`), and the flow table at month 0 must equal the number randomised. Checks like these catch a filter applied in the wrong place.

### Reporting

"Of `r nrow(baseline)` randomised participants, `r sum(grid$observed & grid$month_sched == 12)` (`r round(100 * mean(grid$observed[grid$month_sched == 12]))`%) attended the month-12 visit. Of the `r nrow(grid)` scheduled visits, `r n_missing` were missed: `r n_interm` intermittently and `r n_after` after dropout." The flow table itself belongs in the CONSORT-style participant-flow section of a trial report.

::: {.callout-important title="Common mistakes"}
- **Building the grid from the observed data.** Participants or visits never seen disappear. Build it from the randomisation list and the protocol schedule.
- **Reporting percentages of those seen instead of those randomised.** State the denominator.
- **Testing baseline differences between randomised arms.** Describe them; do not test them.
- **Confusing a missing value at an attended visit with a missed visit.** They have different causes and are counted separately.
:::

## Exploratory plots

```{r}
#| label: walk-lab
walk_lab <- walk |>
  mutate(arm_lab = factor(walk_arm_labels[as.character(arm)],
                          levels = walk_arm_labels))
```

### The research question and estimand

Plots answer questions that tables cannot: How variable are individual trajectories? Do participants differ more in level or in rate of change? Is change linear? Who is missing, and when? Do people who leave look different before they leave? These are the questions that guide the choice of model in later modules [@singer2003; @fitzmaurice2011].

### Data structure and outcome types

Individual-level plots use the long file with actual time on the horizontal axis. Group summaries use scheduled time, because means are computed per visit. The missingness map uses the complete grid built in the previous section.

### Intuition

A **spaghetti plot** draws one line per participant. With hundreds of participants the lines merge into a cloud, so a **random subset** (selected with a fixed seed, never chosen by hand) shows individual shapes. **Individual trajectory panels** give each participant their own small plot. A **group mean plot** summarises each arm at each visit. A **missingness map** shows each participant as a row and each visit as a column. **Pattern plots** show mean profiles separately for groups defined by when participants dropped out.

### The model

The observed group mean plot shows $\bar y_{gj}$ with a 95% confidence interval $\bar y_{gj} \pm t_{0.975,\, n_{gj}-1}\, s_{gj}/\sqrt{n_{gj}}$, where $s_{gj}$ is the standard deviation and $n_{gj}$ the number observed. This interval treats the participants seen at visit $j$ as a simple random sample. It says nothing about correlation between visits, or about who is missing.

### Assumptions and limitations

Plots of observed data show the observed data. A spaghetti plot gives more visual weight to participants who stay longer. Group means are computed on a different set of people at each visit. The pattern plot splits the data into small groups whose means are noisy.

### Fitting the model in R

```{r}
#| label: fig-m02-spaghetti-all
#| fig-cap: "Spaghetti plot of SBP for all 360 participants, by arm. Each line is one participant. Time is actual months since randomisation."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4
plot_spaghetti(walk_lab, month, sbp, id, group = arm_lab, alpha = 0.15) +
  labs(x = "Months since randomisation", y = "SBP (mmHg)")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-m02-spaghetti-subset
#| fig-cap: "Spaghetti plot of a random subset of 30 participants (seed 2)."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4
plot_spaghetti(walk_lab, month, sbp, id, group = arm_lab, n_show = 30,
               seed = 2, alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Months since randomisation", y = "SBP (mmHg)")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-m02-panels
#| fig-cap: "Individual trajectories for four randomly chosen participants per arm."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6
set.seed(4)
panel_ids <- baseline |> group_by(arm) |> slice_sample(n = 4) |> pull(id)
walk_lab |>
  filter(id %in% panel_ids) |>
  ggplot(aes(month, sbp, colour = arm)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 1.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ id, ncol = 4) +
  scale_colour_arm(name = NULL, labels = walk_arm_labels) +
  labs(x = "Months since randomisation", y = "SBP (mmHg)")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-m02-means
#| fig-cap: "Observed mean SBP by arm and scheduled visit, with 95% confidence intervals. Each mean uses only the participants seen at that visit."
plot_observed_means(walk_lab, month_sched, sbp, arm_lab) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = sched_months) +
  labs(x = "Scheduled month", y = "Observed mean SBP (mmHg), 95% CI")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-m02-missmap
#| fig-cap: "Missingness map. Each row is a participant, sorted by last attended visit; dark cells are observed visits."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5
plot_missing_map(grid, id, visit, observed, order_by = last_seen) +
  facet_wrap(~ arm, scales = "free_y", labeller = as_labeller(walk_arm_labels)) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = sched_months) +
  labs(x = "Scheduled month")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-m02-retention
#| fig-cap: "Percentage of randomised participants who have not yet dropped out, by arm."
retention <- grid |>
  group_by(arm, month_sched) |>
  summarise(pct_still_in = 100 * mean(last_seen >= visit))
ggplot(retention, aes(month_sched, pct_still_in, colour = arm)) +
  geom_step(linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point() +
  scale_colour_arm(name = NULL, labels = walk_arm_labels) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = sched_months) +
  labs(x = "Scheduled month", y = "Participants not yet dropped out (%)")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-m02-pattern
#| fig-cap: "Mean observed SBP by dropout pattern (scheduled month of the last attended visit). Point size shows the number of participants. Participants seen only at baseline appear as single points. Every pattern other than 'last seen month 12' contains between 2 and 9 participants per arm."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.5
pattern_means <- walk |>
  left_join(baseline |> select(id, last_month_sched), by = "id",
            relationship = "many-to-one") |>
  mutate(pattern = factor(last_month_sched, levels = sched_months,
                          labels = paste("Last seen month", sched_months))) |>
  group_by(arm, pattern, month_sched) |>
  summarise(mean_sbp = mean(sbp), n = n())
pattern_means |>
  ggplot(aes(month_sched, mean_sbp, colour = pattern)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(aes(size = n)) +
  facet_wrap(~ arm, labeller = as_labeller(walk_arm_labels)) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 3, guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#D55E00", "#E69F00", "#56B4E9", "#009E73",
                                 "#CC79A7", "#222222"), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = sched_months) +
  labs(x = "Scheduled month", y = "Mean observed SBP (mmHg)")
```

The pattern plot is noisy because most dropout patterns contain only a handful of people. A simple numerical summary answers the key question more directly: just before they left, was SBP in those who dropped out higher than in those who stayed? For each visit before month 12, compare each participant's SBP with the mean of their arm at that visit.

```{r}
#| label: dropout-last
dropout_last_sbp <- walk |>
  left_join(baseline |> select(id, last_month_sched), by = "id",
            relationship = "many-to-one") |>
  filter(month_sched < 12) |>
  group_by(arm, month_sched) |>
  mutate(dev_from_mean = sbp - mean(sbp)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(status = if_else(month_sched == last_month_sched,
                          "Last visit before dropout", "Seen again later")) |>
  group_by(status) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_dev = mean(dev_from_mean))
dropout_last_sbp
```

### Interpreting the output

```{r}
#| label: spread-numbers
#| include: false
spread <- walk |> group_by(month_sched) |>
  summarise(q05 = quantile(sbp, 0.05), q95 = quantile(sbp, 0.95))
ret12 <- retention |> filter(month_sched == 12)
```

The full spaghetti plot shows that differences between participants dominate. At every visit the middle 90% of SBP values span roughly `r round(min(spread$q95 - spread$q05))` to `r round(max(spread$q95 - spread$q05))` mmHg, while the arm averages change by a few mmHg. The subset makes individual lines visible. Each participant fluctuates from visit to visit around their own level, which is the within-person variation described in Module 1, and in the programme arms many lines drop during the first months. The individual panels confirm this and show that participants have different numbers of visits, at slightly different times. Mixed models handle both features naturally.

The observed mean plot suggests a fall in SBP in all arms during the first three months, largest in the enhanced programme and smallest in usual care, followed by a plateau. The change is clearly not linear in time, an early sign that the linear-time model of later modules is a simplification and a reason why the primary model uses scheduled visit as a factor.

The missingness map shows the monotone staircase of dropout at the bottom of each panel and scattered intermittent gaps above it. The retention curves are similar in the three arms. By month 12, `r round(ret12$pct_still_in[ret12$arm == "UC"])`% (UC), `r round(ret12$pct_still_in[ret12$arm == "SP"])`% (SP) and `r round(ret12$pct_still_in[ret12$arm == "EP"])`% (EP) of participants had not dropped out. The simulation does include slightly higher dropout in the enhanced programme, but with 120 participants per arm a difference of this size could easily arise by chance, and the curves cross during follow-up.

```{r}
#| label: dropout-numbers
#| include: false
dev_drop <- dropout_last_sbp$mean_dev[dropout_last_sbp$status == "Last visit before dropout"]
n_drop_rows <- dropout_last_sbp$n[dropout_last_sbp$status == "Last visit before dropout"]
sbp0_drop <- baseline |> group_by(dropout) |> summarise(m = mean(sbp0))
```

The dropout summary is the most important result of this section. At their last visit before dropping out, the `r n_drop_rows` participants who later left had SBP on average `r round(dev_drop, 1)` mmHg above the mean of their arm at that visit. Their mean baseline SBP was `r round(sbp0_drop$m[sbp0_drop$dropout], 1)` mmHg, against `r round(sbp0_drop$m[!sbp0_drop$dropout], 1)` mmHg in participants who did not drop out. Dropout is related to the observed outcome. The pattern plot shows the same thing less cleanly. Participants seen only at baseline, and most early-dropout patterns, start above the completers in their arm, although with groups this small some patterns go the other way (for example the few usual-care participants last seen at month 9).

### Checking the model

Use a fixed seed for subsets so the figure can be reproduced, and draw several subsets to make sure the one shown is typical. Check that the number of lines equals the number of participants. Check axis units, and whether the horizontal axis is actual or scheduled time.

### Reporting

"Individual SBP trajectories varied mainly in level, with substantial visit-to-visit fluctuation. Mean SBP fell during the first three months in all arms, most in the enhanced programme. Participants who dropped out had higher SBP at their last attended visit than those who continued (on average `r round(dev_drop, 1)` mmHg above the arm-specific visit mean)."

::: {.callout-important title="Common mistakes"}
- **Choosing "interesting" participants by hand for a subset plot.** Use a random sample with a seed.
- **Plotting scheduled time for individual trajectories.** Use actual time; the scheduled visit is for group summaries.
- **Reading the observed mean plot as the treatment effect.** It mixes treatment effects with changes in who is still measured (next section).
- **Ignoring the missingness plots.** They are the first evidence about the missing-data mechanism.
:::

## Observed means versus model-estimated trajectories

### The research question and estimand

The trial asks how mean SBP would change in each arm if everyone randomised were followed to month 12. The target is $E(Y_{ij})$ for each arm and visit, and the difference in mean change from baseline between arms. The observed mean $\bar{y}_{gj}$ estimates something else: the mean among those still measured at visit $j$, $E(Y_{ij} \mid R_{ij} = 1)$.

### Data structure and outcome types

The long file `walk_long.csv`, with dropout. For teaching only, `walk_complete.csv` contains all `r nrow(load_walk("complete"))` scheduled values, including the ones that went missing. **This comparison is possible only because the data are simulated.** No real study can compute the complete-data mean.

### Intuition

If participants with higher SBP are more likely to leave, the people still measured at month 12 have, on average, lower SBP than the full randomised group would have had. The observed mean is pulled down. A mixed model fitted to all observed data handles this differently. Each participant's early measurements tell the model about that participant's level, and the correlation between visits lets the model use those early values for the later visits that are missing. When dropout depends only on observed values, this is the right thing to do, and the model's estimated means move back towards the complete-data means.

### The model

Under **missing at random (MAR)**, the probability that $y_{ij}$ is missing depends on the observed data (here the last observed SBP and arm) but not on the unobserved value itself, given the observed data [@rubin1976; @little2019]. Even under MAR, in general

$$
E(Y_{ij} \mid R_{ij} = 1) \neq E(Y_{ij}),
$$

because $R_{ij}$ depends on earlier outcomes that are correlated with $Y_{ij}$. The primary WALK model,

$$
y_{ij} = \mathbf{x}_{ij}^\top \boldsymbol\beta + b_{0i} + b_{1i} t_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ij},
$$

with scheduled visit as a factor interacting with arm in $\mathbf{x}_{ij}^\top \boldsymbol\beta$, is fitted by likelihood to all observed $y_{ij}$. Under MAR the likelihood-based estimates of $\boldsymbol\beta$ are valid without modelling the dropout process, provided the model is correctly specified. Modules 4 and 10 explain the model and this result.

### Assumptions and limitations

The comparison relies on MAR, which holds in this simulation by design but can never be verified from observed data. If dropout depended on the unobserved SBP itself (missing not at random), the mixed model would also be biased. Module 10 covers sensitivity analyses for that case. Here we use the model only as a preview.

### Fitting the model in R

```{r}
#| label: obs-vs-model
complete <- load_walk("complete")
m_primary <- lmer(sbp ~ visit_f * arm + (1 + month | id), data = walk,
                  control = lmer_ctrl)
em_visits <- as.data.frame(emmeans(m_primary, ~ visit_f | arm))
means_compare <- complete |>
  group_by(arm, visit_f) |>
  summarise(complete_mean = mean(sbp),
            observed_mean = mean(sbp[observed]),
            n_observed    = sum(observed)) |>
  left_join(em_visits |> select(arm, visit_f, model_mean = emmean),
            by = c("arm", "visit_f")) |>
  mutate(obs_bias   = observed_mean - complete_mean,
         model_bias = model_mean - complete_mean) |>
  ungroup()
means_compare |> filter(visit_f != "0") |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2)))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-m02-obs-vs-model
#| fig-cap: "Mean SBP by arm and scheduled visit from three sources: all scheduled visits (available only because the data are simulated), observed visits only, and the primary mixed model fitted to the observed data."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.5
means_compare |>
  select(arm, visit_f, `All scheduled visits (teaching only)` = complete_mean,
         `Observed visits only` = observed_mean,
         `Mixed model, observed data` = model_mean) |>
  pivot_longer(-c(arm, visit_f), names_to = "source", values_to = "mean") |>
  mutate(month = as.numeric(as.character(visit_f))) |>
  ggplot(aes(month, mean, linetype = source, shape = source)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ arm, labeller = as_labeller(walk_arm_labels)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = sched_months) +
  labs(x = "Scheduled month", y = "Mean SBP (mmHg)", linetype = NULL, shape = NULL)
```

### Interpreting the output

```{r}
#| label: bias-numbers
#| include: false
fu <- means_compare |> filter(visit_f != "0")
n_obs_below <- sum(fu$obs_bias < 0)
change12 <- means_compare |>
  group_by(arm) |>
  summarise(across(c(complete_mean, observed_mean, model_mean),
                   \(x) x[visit_f == "12"] - x[visit_f == "0"]))
f1 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1)
```

The observed mean is below the complete-data mean at `r n_obs_below` of the `r nrow(fu)` follow-up visits, by between `r round(min(-fu$obs_bias), 1)` and `r round(max(-fu$obs_bias), 1)` mmHg. The direction is what the dropout analysis predicted: those who left had higher SBP, so those who remain look healthier. The mixed-model estimates lie much closer to the complete-data means. Their average absolute error over follow-up visits is `r round(mean(abs(fu$model_bias)), 2)` mmHg, against `r round(mean(abs(fu$obs_bias)), 2)` mmHg for the observed means, and their errors go in both directions instead of all one way.

The bias in observed means affects the estimated change from baseline too. In usual care the complete-data change at month 12 is `r f1(change12$complete_mean[1])` mmHg. The observed means give `r f1(change12$observed_mean[1])` mmHg and the model gives `r f1(change12$model_mean[1])` mmHg. In the enhanced programme the corresponding values are `r f1(change12$complete_mean[3])`, `r f1(change12$observed_mean[3])` and `r f1(change12$model_mean[3])` mmHg. The observed means exaggerate the fall in SBP in all three arms. The size of the bias is modest here because dropout was moderate (`r round(100 * mean(baseline$dropout))`% of participants), but it grows with the amount of dropout and with the strength of its dependence on the outcome.

The complete-data means are themselves estimates from 120 participants per arm. They are not the true values in `walk_truth.rds`. The comparison here isolates the effect of missingness. How close each method comes to the truth is a question for later modules.

### Checking the model

Outside a simulation, the comparison of observed and model-estimated means is still informative. If they differ noticeably, and the missingness plots show dropout related to earlier outcomes, the observed means should not be presented as estimates of the arm means. Plot both, and label the observed means as "observed among those seen".

### Reporting

::: {.callout-tip title="Reporting example"}
Observed mean SBP at each visit is reported descriptively with the number of participants contributing. Because participants with higher SBP were more likely to drop out, treatment effects were estimated from a linear mixed model fitted to all observed data, which gives valid estimates when dropout depends on observed values (missing at random). In this simulated example, the observed month-12 mean in the enhanced programme (`r round(means_compare$observed_mean[means_compare$arm == "EP" & means_compare$visit_f == "12"], 1)` mmHg) was lower than the model estimate (`r round(means_compare$model_mean[means_compare$arm == "EP" & means_compare$visit_f == "12"], 1)` mmHg).
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Common mistakes"}
- **Presenting observed visit means as the estimated treatment trajectory.** They describe a shrinking and selected group.
- **Analysing completers only.** This discards information and, under MAR dropout, is biased in the same direction as the observed means.
- **Believing that a mixed model solves every missing-data problem.** It is valid under MAR and correct model specification. Module 10 covers MNAR and sensitivity analyses.
- **Using `walk_complete.csv` in an analysis.** It exists only to show what missingness does. Real studies never have it.
:::

## Summary {.unnumbered}

A longitudinal analysis is only as good as the file it starts from. Reshaping, joining and cleaning are routine operations, but each has a characteristic failure (a time-varying column left in a reshape, a duplicated key in a join, duplicates sought before IDs are standardised), and each can be checked by counting rows and keys before and after. The cleaning decisions that affect outcomes, such as which of two conflicting records to keep, are made by rules fixed in advance and recorded in a log. Once the data are clean, a complete grid built from the design reveals the missing visits, and plots of individual trajectories, group means, missingness and dropout patterns show what the models will have to handle. In WALK they show large differences between people, a nonlinear early fall in SBP, and dropout among participants with higher SBP. That last finding is why observed means at each visit drift below the means of everyone randomised, and why the course estimates trajectories from models fitted to all observed data.

## Further reading {.unnumbered}

- @wickham2014 sets out the principles of tidy data that underlie the long format and the `tidyr` functions.
- @singer2003 (chapter 2) and @fitzmaurice2011 describe exploratory analysis of longitudinal data, including individual trajectory plots.
- @diggle2002, chapter 3, covers graphical exploration of longitudinal data and of the mean and covariance structure.
- @little2019 defines MCAR, MAR and MNAR and explains when likelihood-based analysis of the observed data is valid.
- @gamble2017 lists what a statistical analysis plan should prespecify, including the handling of data and missing values.

## Exercises {.unnumbered}

The workbook `workbook/wb02-data-preparation.qmd` contains guided exercises on reshaping, joining, cleaning a raw export, building the visit grid and drawing the exploratory plots, and independent exercises that apply the same steps to new problems. The practical assessment `assessments/pa02-data-preparation.qmd` asks you to clean and explore a fresh messy export from start to finish.
